Minimizing Collateral Damage in Activation Steering

Tam Nguyen Affiliation: Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering, Rice University, Houston, USA Correspondence to: mn72@rice.edu    Tu Anh Nguyen Affiliation: Department of Computational and Applied Mathematics, Rice University, Houston, USA    Sina Alemohammad Affiliation: Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, USA    Richard G. Baraniuk Affiliation: Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering, Rice University, Houston, USA
Abstract

Activation steering is a method for controlling Large Language Model (LLM) behavior by intervening in its internal representations to increase the alignment with a specific target feature direction. However, standard interventions, such as vector addition, often cause “collateral damage”, defined as unintended changes in the alignment of activations along other non-target feature directions. This damage occurs because standard methods implicitly assume the isotropy of non-target features. In this work, we provide a mathematical formalization of collateral damage and introduce a principled framework that models steering as a constrained optimization problem. Our method finds a new activation that minimizes the expected squared collateral change weighted by the empirical second-moment matrix of activations. This weighting encodes the nonuniform cost of the perturbation in different feature directions, in contrast to isotropic approaches that penalize changes uniformly in all feature directions. By accounting for the empirical second-moment of activations, our approach achieves more precise control while reducing the degradation of model performance on unrelated tasks.

Keywords: 
Activation Steering, Large Language Models, Representation Geometry

1 Introduction

Controlling LLM behavior has traditionally relied on retraining or fine-tuning (Zhang et al., 2026; Ziegler et al., 2019; Dathathri et al., 2020), processes that become increasingly expensive at scale. Activation steering provides a more efficient alternative, enabling behavioral control at inference time without modifying the model weights (Zou et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). By directly intervening in internal representations, this “plug-and-play” approach nudges activation vectors to enhance desirable traits like factuality (Li et al., 2024) or to suppress negative tendencies such as sycophancy, toxicity, and hallucination (Chen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). Recent work has highlighted the broad applicability of activation steering in managing diverse semantic traits—ranging from appropriateness to humor and creativity (Wang et al., 2025a)—demonstrating that alignment can be achieved without costly parameter updates.

A common method for activation steering is ActAdd (Turner et al., 2023), which adds a scaled steering vector directly to a model’s activations. While simple to implement, this class of methods can be scale-sensitive, since the magnitude of the steering vector can significantly alter the model’s internal distribution and lead to performance degradation. Norm-Preserving Steering methods address this by modifying only the activation direction while keeping the original magnitude intact to avoid disrupting the model’s internal scaling (Pham and Nguyen, 2024). Examples include Slerp (for Spherical linear interpolation) (Shoemake, 1985; White, 2016; Jang et al., 2024), which rotates the activation vector along the great circle towards the target direction until the desired cosine similarity is met. Similarly, Angular Steering (Vu and Nguyen, 2025) projects the activation onto a fixed 2D plane and rotates it to a target angle, changing only the in-plane component while preserving the global norm.

Existing steering methods face a trade-off between steering effectiveness and downstream performance. For example, the experiment reported in Figure 3(a) shows that achieving a 30-40% steering success rate with ActAdd causes a 10–20% drop in performance in Gemma-2-9B-IT (Gemma Team et al., 2024). Meanwhile, Angular Steering maintains downstream performance but fails to steer effectively, reaching a success rate of less than 10% in the same model.

The steering/performance trade-off arises because steering the model to exhibit one feature can alter the alignment of the activations with other features. Existing steering methods implicitly treat an activation shift in any direction as equally costly (isotropic). In reality, the geometry of LLM representations is anisotropic. The features are not uniform; some directions are more coupled to others. And when the features are entangled with the steering direction, ignoring this geometry can unintentionally disturb them.

In addition while the general trade-off between steering success and performance has been observed (Zhang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Yousefpour et al., 2025), existing work has focused on heuristic monitoring of downstream benchmarks that address the symptoms of performance loss rather than the geometric root causes.

In this paper, we take initial steps toward understanding and mitigating the tradeoff between activation steering success and model performance. We formalize the concept of collateral damage as the expected unintended alignment shift toward non-target directions and empirically show that increased collateral damage leads to performance degradation (see Fig. 1). Motivated by a geometric view of representation space, we propose a general framework for minimizing collateral damage during steering. Geometrically, given a fixed alignment budget—defined as the cosine similarity between the activation and the target direction— we find the safest steered activation that lies on a particular “latitude” of the hypersphere of normalized activations.

Within this framework, existing activation steering approaches correspond to a special case that we term isotropic collateral damage, where the degradation incurred by steering is assumed to be invariant to the direction of the activation shift and depends only on its magnitude. However, LLM representations are inherently anisotropic; consequently, true collateral damage is direction-dependent and highly sensitive to the geometry of the representation space. This observation motivates explicitly accounting for anisotropy when designing steering methods, which is central to our approach.

We introduce COllateral-damage Minimizing Activation STeering (COAST), which applies algorithms rooted in differential geometry to traverse the solution space and find the optimal steering vector. We prove that COAST converges to the global minimum of the collateral damage objective in the continuous limit. Furthermore, it strictly generalizes SLERP, the norm-preserving version of ActAdd. COAST reduces to SLERP under isotropic conditions but adapts to protect performance when anisotropy is present. Like other additive steering methods, COAST is plug-and-play, adding only a small overhead to the inference cost (e.g., 0.9% to 4% in our experiments).

While baseline methods like ActAdd and Angular Steering exhibit a trade-off between steering effectiveness and model performance—especially in reasoning-intensive tasks included in tinyBenchmarks (Maia Polo et al., 2024)—our experiments demonstrate that COAST effectively mitigates this compromise. Indeed, COAST achieves high-quality steering without degrading performance, yielding up to a 30% improvement in Attack Success Rate (ASR) over Angular Steering and improving up to 20% in accuracy compared to ActAdd at the same ASR. In addition, COAST outperforms SLERP in steering success while preserving the model’s performance.

By explicitly minimizing collateral damage under a fixed steering budget, COAST makes it possible to push models where you want them to go without breaking what already works. This shifts the conversation from “can we steer?” to “can we steer responsibly,” opening the door to deployment settings where reliability, safety, and downstream performance must all be simultaneously protected.

2 Related Work

Activation steering. A growing line of research controls LLM behavior by intervening directly on intermediate activations at inference time (Zou et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). (Turner et al., 2023) formalizes this paradigm as activation engineering and introduces Activation Addition (ActAdd). This method involves computing a steering direction—typically derived from contrastive prompt pairs—and then injecting a scaled version of this vector into the residual stream to shift model attributes. Variants of this approach have been employed to steer behaviors such as truthfulness (Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024) and to modulate persona-style traits like sycophancy, toxicity, and hallucination propensity (Chen et al., 2025). Similarly, (Wang et al., 2025a) applies inference-time steering to control high-level qualities like appropriateness, humor, and creativity. However, a critical drawback of these methods is scale sensitivity: steering quality relies heavily on the intervention coefficient and the effective steering vector norm. This requires careful hyperparameter tuning, and overly strong intervention can degrade fluency or introduce unintended side effects.

Norm-constrained activation steering. (Arditi et al., 2024) introduces directional ablation, which removes the steering vector from the residual stream. By normalizing the steering vector before removal, this method partially mitigates scale sensitivity, though it lacks flexibility as it can only erase the direction, not amplify or attenuate it. Conversely, (Vu and Nguyen, 2025) introduce Angular Steering to promote norm-preservation and flexibility. This method constructs a 2D plane using the steering vector and the first principal component of the steering vectors across all layers, performing rotation on this plane while preserving the activation components orthogonal to it. However, because the rotation is restricted to a fixed 2D plane, Angular Steering struggles to satisfy specific alignment budgets, can leads to struggle in steering success. Furthermore, Angular Steering relies on the assumption that features are nearly orthogonal. In Section 3.4, we demonstrate that, when this assumption holds, Spherical Linear Interpolation (Slerp) is the optimal solution for minimizing collateral damage. Generalizing beyond this constraint, COAST achieves the global optimum solution given an alignment budget.

Robust activation steering. Prior work has highlighted a trade-off between safety and utility, as activation steering can cause over-refusal and degrade model usefulness (Zhang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Yousefpour et al., 2025). Mitigation strategies include conditional activation steering (Lee et al., 2025), sharpening target direction (Wang et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2025), or nullspace-constrained approaches (Wang et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2025) that dynamically induce refusal only for malicious prompts. Our work generalizes the goal of activation steering beyond safety to the broader challenge of altering any attribute without compromising overall performance. Our approach is orthogonal to these robust methods focusing explicitly on formulating and minimizing collateral damage during steering.

3 Collateral-damage Minimizing Activation Steering (COAST)

In this paper we study normalized activation steering: we edit a representation while preserving its magnitude, and we choose the intervention to minimize collateral damage subject to a directional alignment budget. The steering direction serves as a simple control knob, i.e., an explicit constraint on how far the intervention may deviate from the intended steering direction. Concretely, we enforce this budget by lower-bounding the cosine similarity between the intervention vector and the steering direction. This formulation naturally treats features as directions in activation space, aligning with the linear feature hypothesis (Park et al., 2024; Nanda et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024) and enabling principled, geometry-aware steering.

3.1 Steering with an alignment budget

Let 𝐡∈ℝp\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} denote the activation, and let 𝐝∈ℝp\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} denote a target feature direction. We seek a new activation 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} that satisfies a prescribed alignment budget 𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha, where α∈[−1,1]\alpha\in[-1,1] is the desired post-steering cosine similarity with 𝐝\mathbf{d}. We also enforce norm preservation by working on the unit sphere and assuming that ‖𝐡‖=‖𝐝‖=1\|\mathbf{h}\|=\|\mathbf{d}\|=1 and ‖𝐱‖=1\|\mathbf{x}\|=1. This normalization is without loss of generality, since we can rescale the steered activation by its original activation norm after the intervention.

We begin by formulating an objective that explicitly quantifies the impact of steering on non-target features. To this end, we model non-target features as belong to the family ℱ={𝐟∈ℝp∣𝐟≠𝐝, 𝐟 is semantic}\mathcal{F}=\{\mathbf{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\mid\mathbf{f}\neq\mathbf{d},\text{ }\mathbf{f}\text{ is semantic}\}, representing all meaningful directions excluding the target. We measure the collateral change induced by steering as the change in alignment along 𝐟\mathbf{f}, given by 𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡)\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}). We define the collateral damage as the expected squared collateral change over the population of non-target feature directions

𝔼⁡[(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2]=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺𝐟​(𝐱−𝐡),\mathbb{E}\big[(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}\big]\;=\;(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}), (1)

where the expectation is summarized by the second moment matrix 𝚺𝐟:=𝔼⁡[𝐟𝐟⊤]\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{f}}:=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^{\top}] that we dub the collateral weighting matrix.

Combining the fixed-norm constraint and the alignment budget defines the feasible set

ℳ:={𝐱∈ℝp:∥𝐱∥=1,𝐝⊤𝐱=α}.\mathcal{M}\;:=\;\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\|\mathbf{x}\|=1,\;\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha\}. (2)

Our steering problem is therefore the constrained optimization

min𝐱∈ℳ⁡(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺𝐟​(𝐱−𝐡).\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}). (3)

The solution to (3) achieves the required steering effect with minimal collateral damage.

3.2 Choosing the collateral weighting matrix 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma}

The collateral matrix 𝚺𝐟=𝔼⁡[𝐟𝐟⊤]\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{f}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^{\top}] specifies which feature directions are costly to perturb. Specifically, 𝚺𝐟\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{f}} treats feature directions as uniformly important—meaning a change along feature fif_{i} is just as costly as a change along feature fjf_{j}.

However, it is crucial to note that treating features with equal importance does not imply that the optimization landscape is isotropic (i.e., that steering costs are the same in all ambient directions). For example, if features are clustered—as is common in LLMs—steering toward a cluster disturbs many features simultaneously, creating high-cost directions. To clarify this distinction, we introduce the following.

Remark 1 (Two notions of uniformity).

We distinguish between two distinct types of uniformity that govern the behavior of activation steering.

Uniform importance relates to our prescriptive intent; it assumes that every non-target feature direction should be penalized equally. This leads to an unweighted objective where the collateral matrix Σf\Sigma_{f} considers all directions to be of equal functional concern.

Uniform geometric distribution relates to the descriptive property of the latent space; it assumes that feature directions themselves are distributed uniformly (isotropically) on the unit sphere.

In practice, applications often require feature-preservation prioritization that is task-dependent or user-specific. Therefore, we generalize the notion of 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} to an abstract collateral matrix. Different choices of 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} encode different notions of feature preservation and can reflect task-dependent or user-specific requirements.

We generalize the unweighted expectation by introducing a weighted objective that incorporates a feature importance function w⁡(𝐟)≥0w(\mathbf{f})\geq 0. The resulting collateral objective is defined as 𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝐟)​(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2]=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺w​(𝐱−𝐡)\mathbb{E}[w(\mathbf{f})(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}]=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{w}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}), where the collateral weighting matrix is 𝚺w:=𝔼⁡[w⁡(𝐟)​𝐟𝐟⊤]\mathbf{\Sigma}_{w}:=\mathbb{E}[w(\mathbf{f})\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^{\top}]. Unlike standard isotropic methods that assign equal weight to all perturbations, this formulation enables explicit collateral preservation based on specific functional preferences. By adjusting w⁡(𝐟)w(\mathbf{f}), practitioners can prioritize the protection of certain semantic directions over others, moving beyond the limiting assumption of uniform significance across the feature landscape

The primary optimization challenge is that the latent feature family ℱ\mathcal{F} is not enumerable, making direct computation of 𝚺w\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w} infeasible. A natural approximation is to represent features using a learned dictionary 𝐅=[𝐟1,…,𝐟m]\mathbf{F}=[\mathbf{f}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{f}_{m}] via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) (Ng and others, 2011; Gao et al., 2025; Lieberum et al., 2024). To quantify feature importance, one approach is utilize a distribution of reference activations, ℋref\mathcal{H}_{\text{ref}}, collected by passing a general text corpus through the model. Since SAEs decompose any activation 𝐡∈ℋref\mathbf{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{ref}} as 𝐡≈∑ici​(𝐡)​𝐟i\mathbf{h}\approx\sum_{i}c_{i}(\mathbf{h})\mathbf{f}_{i}, we can define the importance weight wi=𝔼𝐡∼ℋref​[ci​(𝐡)2]w_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{h}\sim\mathcal{H}_{\text{ref}}}[c_{i}(\mathbf{h})^{2}]. This formulation ensures that features used frequently or strongly across the general data distribution are penalized more heavily. This yields the dictionary-based collateral weighting matrix 𝚺w=∑iwi​𝐟i​𝐟i⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{w}=\sum_{i}w_{i}\mathbf{f}_{i}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}. While interpretable, this construction introduces substantial overhead, as it requires training high-quality SAEs for every model and layer of interest.

More fundamentally, the dictionary-based approach is limited because it ignores feature interactions. By summing over individual-feature moments, it implicitly assumes that features are statistically independent, thereby treating interaction terms as zero. In reality, however, features can co-activate (Deng et al., 2025). To respect the feature geometry without relying on explicit decomposition, we propose using the empirical second moment of the activations, 𝚺𝐡ref=𝔼𝐡∼ℋref​[𝐡ref​𝐡ref⊤]\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{h}\sim\mathcal{H}_{\text{ref}}}[\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}^{\top}], as the collateral weighting matrix. Unlike the dictionary-based approximation, this metric rigorously aggregates both individual feature moments and their co-activation terms:

𝚺𝐡ref=𝔼⁡[𝐡ref​𝐡refT]≈𝔼⁡[∑ici2​𝐟i​𝐟iT+∑i≠jci​cj​𝐟i​𝐟jT],\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}^{T}]\approx\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i}c_{i}^{2}\mathbf{f}_{i}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{T}+\sum_{i\neq j}c_{i}c_{j}\mathbf{f}_{i}\mathbf{f}_{j}^{T}\right],

where ci=ci​(𝐡ref)c_{i}=c_{i}(\mathbf{h}_{\text{ref}}), and cj=cj​(𝐡ref)c_{j}=c_{j}(\mathbf{h}_{\text{ref}}). By adopting 𝚺𝐡ref\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}}, COAST can account for anisotropic feature correlations and co-activations without requiring explicit feature decomposition or external dictionaries. In practice, the empirical second moment 𝚺𝐡ref\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}} can be computed using NN tokens sampled from a general-purpose corpus or a domain-specific dataset relevant to the target task.

Henceforth, we will use 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} to denote a general collateral weighting matrix; we will specify 𝚺𝐟\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{f}}, 𝚺w\mathbf{\Sigma}_{w}, or 𝚺𝐡ref\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}} only when the distinction is necessary.

3.3 COAST optimization on the budget sphere ℳ\mathcal{M}

We now develop an algorithm to efficiently solve the constrained optimization problem min𝐱∈ℳ⁡J⁡(𝐱)\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}J(\mathbf{x}), where J⁡(𝐱)=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)J(\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}) is the collateral damage and ℳ\mathcal{M} is the feasible set from (2).

Geometry of the feasible set. The budget constraint 𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha fixes a target latitude on the unit sphere. Consequently, the feasible set ℳ\mathcal{M} defined in (2) forms a (p−2)(p-2)-sphere with center α​𝐝\alpha\mathbf{d} and radius r=1−α2r=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}. This geometric perspective naturally motivates the use of Riemannian optimization.

3.3.1 Tangent space and Riemannian gradient on ℳ\mathcal{M}

To adopt techniques from Riemannian optimization, we first need to characterize the tangent space T𝐱​ℳT_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M} for any 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}. A vector 𝝃∈ℝP\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{P} is tangent to the manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} at 𝐱\mathbf{x} if an infinitesimal step from 𝐱\mathbf{x} along a curve on ℳ\mathcal{M} with initial velocity 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} does not violate the optimization constraints. This implies 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} must be orthogonal to the gradients of the constraint functions c1​(𝐱)≔12​(‖𝐱‖2−1)c_{1}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\tfrac{1}{2}(\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}-1) and c2​(𝐱)≔𝐝⊤​𝐱−αc_{2}(\mathbf{x})\coloneqq\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}-\alpha. Since ∇c1​(𝐱)=𝐱\nabla c_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x} and ∇c2​(𝐱)=𝐝\nabla c_{2}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{d}, we have

T𝐱ℳ={𝝃∈ℝP:𝐱⊤𝝃=0,𝐝⊤𝝃=0}.T_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}=\{\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{P}:\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0,\ \mathbf{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0\}. (4)

Tangent-space projector. Let Π𝐱\Pi_{\mathbf{x}} denote the orthogonal projector onto T𝐱​ℳT_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}. Since the normal space of T𝐱​ℳT_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M} is the span of {𝐱,𝐝}\{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{d}\}, the unique symmetric projector with range T𝐱​ℳT_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M} is given by

Π𝐱=𝐈−𝐱𝐱⊤−(𝐝−α​𝐱)​(𝐝−α​𝐱)⊤1−α2.\Pi_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}-\frac{(\mathbf{d}-\alpha\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{d}-\alpha\mathbf{x})^{\top}}{1-\alpha^{2}}.

Here, 𝐝−α​𝐱\mathbf{d}-\alpha\mathbf{x} is the component of 𝐝\mathbf{d} orthogonal to 𝐱\mathbf{x} and ‖𝐝−α​𝐱‖2=1−α2=r2\|\mathbf{d}-\alpha\mathbf{x}\|^{2}=1-\alpha^{2}=r^{2}.

Riemannian gradient. The Euclidean gradient of J⁡(𝐱)J(\mathbf{x}) is ∇J​(𝐱)=2​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)\nabla J(\mathbf{x})=2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}). Projecting ∇J​(𝐱)\nabla J(\mathbf{x}) onto the tangent space yields the Riemannian gradient, we derive the steepest-ascent direction on ℳ\mathcal{M} as

gradJ(𝐱)=Π𝐱∇J(𝐱)=Π𝐱(2𝚺(𝐱−𝐡)).\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x})=\Pi_{\mathbf{x}}\nabla J(\mathbf{x})=\Pi_{\mathbf{x}}\big(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\big). (5)

Based on (5), the underlying idea of the COAST optimization algorithm in Alg. 1 is to minimize JJ by descending along −grad,J⁡(𝐱)-\mathrm{grad},J(\mathbf{x}) while remaining on the feasible set ℳ\mathcal{M}.

3.3.2 Geodesic update via the exponential map

Given 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}, we take a tangent step 𝐯=−η​grad​J​(𝐱)∈T𝐱​ℳ\mathbf{v}=-\eta\,\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x})\in T_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M} and update by following the manifold geodesic defined by the exponential map exp𝐱⁡(𝐯)\exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v}). Because ℳ\mathcal{M} is a sphere of radius rr centered at α​𝐝\alpha\mathbf{d}, this map has a closed form as expressed in Lemma 1.

Lemma 1 (Exponential map on ℳ\mathcal{M}).

Let 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} and 𝐯∈T𝐱​ℳ\mathbf{v}\in T_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}. The geodesic step from 𝐱\mathbf{x} in direction 𝐯\mathbf{v} is

exp𝐱⁡(𝐯)=α​𝐝+(𝐱−α​𝐝)​cos⁡(τ)+r​𝐯‖𝐯‖​sin⁡(τ),\exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v})\;=\;\alpha\mathbf{d}+(\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf{d})\cos(\tau)\;+\;r\,\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}\sin(\tau), (6)

where τ=‖𝐯‖/r\tau=\|\mathbf{v}\|/r and r=1−α2r=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.2.

Optimization algorithm. Essentially, Lemma 1 provides a mechanism for moving in the direction of −grad​J​(𝐱)-\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}) while remaining on the (p−2)(p-2)-sphere ℳ\mathcal{M}. This completes the final component of COAST. As we see in Algorithm 1, COAST first initializes to a point 𝐱0∈ℳ\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathcal{M} and then iteratively performs geodesic updates along the negative Riemannian gradient.

Remark 2 (Geometric interpretation: Safe landing in target latitude).

Geometrically, the alignment constraint d⊤​x=αd^{\top}x=\alpha restricts the feasible set ℳ\mathcal{M} to a specific “latitude” on the (p−2)(p-2)-sphere. Our optimization algorithm interprets this latitude as a standalone manifold and searches for the “safest landing spot” for the steered activation xx. Crucially, by utilizing intrinsic geodesic steps, COAST ensures that the prescribed alignment budget is satisfied exactly at every iteration while simultaneously minimizing the collateral damage. The collateral weighting matrix Σ\Sigma acts as a Riemannian metric that deforms the search space; it induces a “functional topography” of ridges and valleys, where movement into sensitive, high-variance feature directions is penalized, effectively guiding the steered activation toward the safest available representation.

Alternative solver via KKT. We refer interested readers to Appendix E for details on solving the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system associated with problem (3). In brief, the KKT conditions reduce to a single-variable root-finding problem. By exhaustively enumerating all roots, one can guarantee the global optimum of (3). While this approach provides valuable theoretical insights, its practical applicability is limited. As demonstrated in our experiments in Section 5, an approximate solution to (3) is sufficient and enables significantly faster computation.

3.4 COAST/Slerp equivalence

While COAST is a strict generalization of Slerp, when the collateral damage (1) is isotropic, COAST reduces to Slerp and so attains the same performance. COAST provides a unified framework: it recovers Slerp, the norm-preserving counterpart of ActAdd, in the isotropic collateral damage case, yet it correctly adapts the steering solution when collateral damage is anisotropic.

Definition 1 (Isotropic Collateral Damage (ICD)).

The collateral damage J⁡(𝚫)=𝚫T​𝚺​𝚫J(\boldsymbol{\Delta})=\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\Delta} from (1), where 𝚫:=𝐱−𝐡\boldsymbol{\Delta}:=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}, is isotropic if it is invariant to the direction of Δ\Delta, i.e., J⁡(𝚫1)=J⁡(𝚫2)if‖𝚫1‖2=‖𝚫2‖2J(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{1})=J(\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{2})\quad\text{if}\quad\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{1}\|_{2}=\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{2}\|_{2}. Otherwise, JJ is anisotropic.

Here are three scenarios when ICD can occur.

Scenario 1: Worst-case damage and features are orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}. When the non-target features are orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}, i.e., the collateral weighting is isotropic within the subspace orthogonal to the target direction 𝐝\mathbf{d}, this is equivalent to choosing 𝚺=Π𝐝⟂:=(𝐈−𝐝𝐝T)\mathbf{\Sigma}=\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}:=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^{T}).

This situation is mathematically equivalent to minimizing the worst-case collateral damage, where the objective is the supremum of the change over all unit features 𝐟\mathbf{f} orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}:

min𝐱∈ℳsup𝐟:‖𝐟‖=1,𝐝T​𝐟=0{𝐟T(𝐱−𝐡)}2⇔min𝐱∈ℳ⁡‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2.\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\sup_{\mathbf{f}:\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\mathbf{d}^{T}\mathbf{f}=0}\left\{\mathbf{f}^{T}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\right\}^{2}\\ \iff\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}.

This problem admits a unique, closed-form solution. The optimal point 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} is the one on the manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} that lies within the two-dimensional plane spanned by 𝐡\mathbf{h} and 𝐝\mathbf{d}:

𝐱∗=α​𝐝+r​𝐡−(𝐝T​𝐡)​𝐝‖𝐡−(𝐝T​𝐡)​𝐝‖,\mathbf{x}^{*}=\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\frac{\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{T}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{T}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}\|}, (7)

where r=1−α2r=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}. This solution is a Slerp from 𝐡\mathbf{h} toward 𝐝\mathbf{d}, stopped at the point where the alignment budget 𝐝T​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{T}\mathbf{x}=\alpha is met.

Scenario 2: Worst-case damage and features are nearly orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}. Motivated by the superposition hypothesis (Elhage et al., 2022), one can relax the strict orthogonality condition 𝐝⊤​𝐟=0\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{f}=0 to allow a small overlap: |𝐝⊤​𝐟|≤ε|\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{f}|\leq\varepsilon for some small positive ε\varepsilon. Consider the corresponding worst-case collateral objective

min𝐱∈ℳsup𝐟:‖𝐟‖=1,|𝐝⊤​𝐟|≤ε{𝐟⊤(𝐱−𝐡)}2.\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\ \sup_{\mathbf{f}:\ \|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\ |\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{f}|\leq\varepsilon}\left\{\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\right\}^{2}. (8)

On the budget sphere ℳ\mathcal{M}, the change along the target direction 𝐝\mathbf{d} is fixed 𝐝⊤​(𝐱−𝐡)=α−𝐝⊤​𝐡.\mathbf{d}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})=\alpha-\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h}. As a result, the supremum in (8) depends on 𝐱\mathbf{x} only through the change in the orthogonal complement of 𝐝\mathbf{d}, which is ‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|. Hence, the minimizer is identical to the orthogonal case, and the optimal solution remains the same closed-form Slerp point in span​{𝐡,𝐝}\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{h},\mathbf{d}\} given in (7). The full derivation is given in Appendix B.2.

Scenario 3: Uniform-on-sphere features. If the collateral empirical features are distributed uniformly on the sphere Sp−1S^{p-1}, then the collateral weighting matrix is proportional to the identity, 𝚺∝𝐈\mathbf{\Sigma}\propto\mathbf{I}. The objective then simplifies to minimizing the squared Euclidean distance, J⁡(𝐱)∝‖𝐱−𝐡‖2J(\mathbf{x})\propto\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}\|^{2}.

Similarly, minimizing this objective on the budget slice 𝐝T​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{T}\mathbf{x}=\alpha is achieved by the same one-shot geodesic: a rotation of 𝐡\mathbf{h} toward 𝐝\mathbf{d} along the great circle until the constraint is met. The full derivation is given in Appendix B.3.

4 Theoretical analysis of COAST

This section establishes optimization guarantees for COAST in the general anisotropic collateral damage. Although the collateral damage objective J⁡(𝐱)=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)J(\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}) is quadratic in the ambient space, the feasible set ℳ\mathcal{M} is a curved manifold, and so closed-form solutions are unavailable beyond the three ICD scenarios discussed above. We first show that the continuous-time Riemannian gradient flow converges to a single stationary point, and then show that with the geometric initialization used in Algorithm 1, the flow converges to the global optimum.

Lemma 2 (Convergence of gradient flow on the spherical slice).

Let ℳ={𝐱∈ℝp∣∥𝐱∥=1,𝐝⊤𝐱=α}\mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\mid\|\mathbf{x}\|=1,\ \mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha\}, where ‖𝐝‖=1\|\mathbf{d}\|=1 and |α|<1|\alpha|<1. Consider J⁡(𝐱)=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)J(\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}), where 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} is symmetric PSD. Let 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) be the solution to the Riemannian gradient flow on ℳ\mathcal{M},

𝐱˙​(t)=−grad​J​(𝐱⁡(t)),𝐱⁡(0)∈ℳ.\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)=-\mathrm{grad}\,J(\mathbf{x}(t)),\qquad\mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathcal{M}.

Then 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) converges to a single critical point 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} as t→∞t\to\infty.

In the three ICD cases, the COAST objective reduces to a metric proportional to 𝐈\mathbf{I} or Π𝐝⟂\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}} and admits a one-shot SLERP solution. In the general anisotropic case, the manifold constraints prevent a closed-form update, and we instead optimize using Riemannian gradient descent. The next theorem shows that the continuous-time flow converges to the global optimum when initialized at the Euclidean projection of 𝐡\mathbf{h} onto the budget manifold. The full proof of Lemma 2 is provided in Appendix A.1.

Theorem 1 (Global convergence to optimal steering).

Let 𝚺∈ℝp×p\mathbf{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} be symmetric PSD, and consider the same optimization problem in Lem. 2 min𝐱∈ℳ⁡J⁡(𝐱)\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}J(\mathbf{x}). Let 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) solve the Riemannian gradient flow 𝐱˙​(t)=−grad​J​(𝐱​(t))\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)=-\mathrm{grad}\,J(\mathbf{x}(t)), and 𝐱⁡(0)=𝐱0\mathbf{x}(0)=\mathbf{x}_{0} initialized at the Euclidean projection of 𝐡\mathbf{h} onto ℳ\mathcal{M},

𝐱0=α​𝐝+r​𝐡−(𝐝⊤​𝐡)​𝐝‖𝐡−(𝐝⊤​𝐡)​𝐝‖,r=1−α2.\mathbf{x}_{0}=\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\,\frac{\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}\|},\qquad r=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}.

Then 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) converges to the global minimizer 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} of JJ on ℳ\mathcal{M} as t→∞t\to\infty.

The proof of Theorem 1 is provided in Appendix A.3.

Step-size selection. Since Algorithm 1 discretizes the continuous flow of Theorem 1 via Riemannian gradient descent, we next derive step-size bounds for the exponential map that guarantee objective decrease and solver stability.

Proposition 1 (Choice of step-size).

Consider the same objective and manifold constraints in Thm. 1. Let Π𝐝⟂:=I−𝐝𝐝⊤\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}:=I-\mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^{\top} denote the orthogonal projector onto the subspace orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}. Following Alg. 1, the Riemannian gradient descent update given by 𝐱t+1=exp𝐱t⁡(η​𝛏t)\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\exp_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}(\eta\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{t}) (as in (6)), where 𝛏t=−grad​J​(𝐱t)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{t}=-\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t}), where grad​J\mathrm{grad}J denotes the Riemannian gradient on ℳ\mathcal{M}. The function JJ is geodesically LL-smooth with Lipschitz constant L=2​‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂‖2L=2\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\|_{2}. Consequently, the iterates satisfy the descent inequality J⁡(𝐱t+1)≤J⁡(𝐱t)−η2​‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖2J(\mathbf{x}_{t+1})\leq J(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\frac{\eta}{2}\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}, for any step size satisfying

0<η≤1L0<\eta\leq\frac{1}{L} (9)

The proof of Proposition 1 is given in Appendix A.4.

Proposition 1 implies that, with sufficiently small step-size, COAST makes consistent progress whenever the gradient is non-zero. Accumulating this progress over a finite horizon TT, we derive a sublinear convergence rate to a stationary point (see Appendix A.5).

5 Experiments

In this section, we demonstrate the effectiveness of COAST across a diverse set of instruction-tuned LLMs spanning various families and scales: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), and Gemma-2-9B-IT (Gemma Team et al., 2024). We compare against four baselines: ActAdd, Angular Steering, Slerp, and No Steering.

To assess steering effectiveness, we define the Attack Success Rate (ASR) as the fraction of harmful instructions for which the steered model successfully produces a jailbreak completion (higher indicates stronger steering). We compute the ASR using HarmBench, a standardized evaluation framework for automated red teaming and robust refusal.

To evaluate performance preservation, we report task accuracy on the tinyBenchmarks suite of tasks (Maia Polo et al., 2024), including 100 examples of ARC (Clark et al., 2018), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), Winogrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), and HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019).

Appendix C contains the experimental details: (i) intervention locations (Appendix C.2), (ii) target direction construction (Appendix C.3), (iii) collateral matrix estimation and optimization hyperparameters (Appendix C.4), (iv) steering strength (Appendix C.6), (v) adaptive alignment budgets (Appendix C.7) (vi) norm-preserving implementation (Appendix C.8).

Trade-off between jailbreak success and general capability. We plot ASR against Task Accuracy to evaluate the ability of steering methods to compel harmful compliance while minimizing capability degradation. As shown in Fig. 3, ActAdd exhibits a steep trade-off—sacrificing accuracy to achieve ASR—while Angular Steering struggles to yield high ASR. In contrast, COAST consistently drives high ASR while maintaining task performance comparable to unsteered models. Effectively, COAST achieves robust steering with minimal overhead, delivering up to a 30% improvement in ASR over Angular Steering and a 20% accuracy advantage over ActAdd at equivalent ASR levels.

Comparison with Slerp. We compare COAST to Slerp by averaging metrics across steering intensities θ∈[0∘,180∘]\theta\in[0^{\circ},180^{\circ}] (see App. C.6). Table 1 demonstrates that COAST achieves a higher Alignment Success Rate (ASR) across three of the four evaluated models. For Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.2-3B specifically, COAST improves both ASR and task accuracy simultaneously. In cases where Slerp retains slightly higher accuracy, the margin is small, suggesting that COAST increases steering efficacy without capability degradation.

Theoretically, as a generalization of Slerp, COAST should perform at least as well as the baseline. We hypothesize that instances where Slerp slightly outperforms COAST are attributable to optimization dynamics. In regions where the collateral damage is nearly isotropic—where Slerp provides the exact closed-form solution—COAST approximates this solution via gradient descent. Consequently, with aggressive step sizes, the optimization may occasionally deviate from the optimal path, a limitation resolvable with finer hyperparameter tuning.

Computational Efficiency. We evaluated efficiency by measuring inference throughput in tokens/second. COAST incurs a marginal overhead, slower than the unsteered baseline by 0.9%–4.0% and than the Slerp baseline by less than 1.5%. Detailed results are provided in Appendix D and Table 2.

Analysis: Collateral damage as proxy measure of performance degradation. To validate collateral damage as a proxy for performance degradation, we evaluated ActAdd and COAST on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with the tinyBenchmarks. For each task, we computed the collateral damage—defined as (𝐱−𝐡)T​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})—averaged over all layers and activations. Each point in Fig. 1 represents a steering method applied with different steering coefficients (see Appendix C.6), plotted against its corresponding downstream accuracy. We observe a strong negative Pearson correlation (r<−0.9r<-0.9) across all tasks, confirming that our metric is a reliable predictor of model performance decline.

6 Conclusions

COAST turns activation steering from an ad hoc editing trick into a principled, geometry-aware control method: for a chosen steering direction, it finds the least disruptive norm-preserving intervention that still achieves a specified alignment budget. By explicitly modeling anisotropy through the empirical second-moment structure, COAST replaces the hidden isotropy assumption behind many steering operators with a metric that reflects which directions in activation space are actually costly to perturb (causing collateral damage). This yields a practical steering regime that improves the effectiveness–capability tradeoff, enabling targeted behavior changes without sacrificing unrelated competencies. More broadly, COAST provides a foundation for accountable activation interventions (steering with explicit objectives, transparent constraints, and predictable side effects) that bring behavior control closer to something we can deploy with confidence.

Impact Statement

This paper contributes to safer and more reliable use of large language models by reducing unintended side effects of activation steering. By explicitly optimizing for minimal collateral change under a fixed steering budget, COAST helps prevent capability degradation and unexpected behavioral drift when deploying steering-based controls for alignment, personalization, or content moderation. Our method can lower the risk of overbroad interventions that suppress helpful behaviors or amplify spurious ones, supporting more predictable model behavior in real-world systems. At the same time, steering remains a powerful intervention tool that could be misused to elicit harmful or deceptive behaviors; we therefore emphasize evaluation across diverse tasks, transparent reporting of side effects, and responsible access controls for deployment.

A.1 Proof of Lem. 2 (Convergence of Gradient Flow on Spherical Slice)

J⁡(𝐱)=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)J(\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}) over ℳ:={𝐱:∥𝐱∥=1,𝐝⊤𝐱=α}\mathcal{M}:=\{\mathbf{x}:\|\mathbf{x}\|=1,\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha\}.

Consider any 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} and any orthogonal basis {𝐞1,𝐞2,…,𝐞p−2}\{\mathbf{e}_{1},\mathbf{e}_{2},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{p-2}\} of T𝐱​ℳT_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}.

Define grad ​J​(𝐱)=∑i=1p−2d​J𝐱​(𝐞i)​𝐞i∈T𝐱​ℳ\text{grad }J(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}dJ_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{e}_{i})\mathbf{e}_{i}\in T_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}.

Let 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) solve the gradient flow ODE on ℳ\mathcal{M}:

𝐱˙​(t)=−grad ​J​(𝐱​(t))\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)=-\text{grad }J(\mathbf{x}(t))

Then 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) converges to a single point as t→∞t\to\infty.

Proof:

Claim 1: JJ is non-increasing.

Proof:

dd​tJ(𝐱(t))=dJ𝐱⁡(t)(𝐱˙(t))=dJ𝐱⁡(t)(−∑i=1p−2dJ𝐱(𝐞i)𝐞i)\frac{d}{dt}J(\mathbf{x}(t))=dJ_{\mathbf{x}(t)}(\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t))=dJ_{\mathbf{x}(t)}\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}dJ_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{e}_{i})\mathbf{e}_{i}\right)
=∑i=1p−2−dJ𝐱(𝐞i)2⟨𝐞i,𝐞i⟩g(since ∥𝐞i∥=1)=\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}-dJ_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{e}_{i})^{2}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{e}_{i}\rangle_{g}\quad(\text{since }\|\mathbf{e}_{i}\|=1)
=⟨grad ​J𝐱​(t),−grad ​J𝐱​(t)⟩=−‖grad ​J𝐱​(t)‖2≤0=\langle\text{grad }J_{\mathbf{x}}(t),-\text{grad }J_{\mathbf{x}}(t)\rangle=-\|\text{grad }J_{\mathbf{x}}(t)\|^{2}\leq 0

Since ℳ\mathcal{M} is a p−2p-2 sphere, it is closed and bounded. ℳ\mathcal{M} is compact. Hence any infinite sequence in ℳ\mathcal{M} must have at least one accumulation point in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Since 𝐱⁡(t)∈ℳ\mathbf{x}(t)\in\mathcal{M} for all tt, the sequence 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) has at least one accumulation point.

Let Ω\Omega be the set containing all accumulation points of 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t).

Claim 2: Ω\Omega is non-empty, compact, connected.

Proof:

  • •

    Non-empty: (above discussion, because ℳ\mathcal{M} is compact).

  • •

    Compact: Let {yn}\{y_{n}\} be a convergent sequence in Ω\Omega (if there is any). Since y1∈Ωy_{1}\in\Omega, we can find t1t_{1} s.t. 𝐱⁡(t1)\mathbf{x}(t_{1}) is arbitrarily close to y1y_{1}. For y2y_{2}, we can find t2>t1t_{2}>t_{1} s.t. 𝐱⁡(t2)\mathbf{x}(t_{2}) is arbitrarily close to y2y_{2}, and so on. Hence the sequence 𝐱⁡(t1),𝐱⁡(t2),…\mathbf{x}(t_{1}),\mathbf{x}(t_{2}),\dots gets infinitely close to {y1,y2,…}\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots\}. But {yn}\{y_{n}\} converges to yy. Meanwhile {𝐱⁡(t1),𝐱⁡(t2),…}\{\mathbf{x}(t_{1}),\mathbf{x}(t_{2}),\dots\} is a subsequence of 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t), hence its limit is in Ω\Omega. Therefore Ω\Omega is closed. And a closed subset of a compact set is also compact.

  • •

    Connected: Suppose Ω\Omega is disconnected. WLOG, assume Ω=Ω1∪Ω2\Omega=\Omega_{1}\cup\Omega_{2}, Ω1∩Ω2=∅\Omega_{1}\cap\Omega_{2}=\emptyset. Since p1∈Ω1,p2∈Ω2p_{1}\in\Omega_{1},p_{2}\in\Omega_{2} are accumulation points of 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t), 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) goes arbitrarily near p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} infinite times. Hence 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) goes through the space between Ω1,Ω2\Omega_{1},\Omega_{2} infinite times. Since that middle set is also compact, a limit of the infinite subsequence of 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) in that set also has an accumulation point in that set. 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) has an accumulation point in that set, which also must be in Ω\Omega. So by contradiction, Ω\Omega must be connected.

Note that ℳ\mathcal{M} is compact and positive invariant w.r.t 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) (Because the entire trajectory stays in ℳ\mathcal{M} from start t0→∞t_{0}\to\infty). Also notice that dd​t​J​(𝐱⁡(t))≤0∀t\frac{d}{dt}J(\mathbf{x}(t))\leq 0\quad\forall t. Let the set of critical points be:

E={𝐱⁡(t)∈ℳ∣grad ​J​(𝐱⁡(t))=0}E=\{\mathbf{x}(t)\in\mathcal{M}\mid\text{grad }J(\mathbf{x}(t))=0\}

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the largest Positive invariant set in EE such that all trajectories starting in ℐ\mathcal{I} will stay in ℐ\mathcal{I} forever. By LaSalle’s Invariance Principle, 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) (as starting in ℳ\mathcal{M}) will approach ℐ\mathcal{I} as t→∞t\to\infty. Hence the accumulation-point set Ω⊆ℐ⊆E\Omega\subseteq\mathcal{I}\subseteq E.

Claim 3: EE is finite.

Proof: The problem becomes:

min(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)s.t.‖𝐱‖=1,𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\min\quad(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|\mathbf{x}\|=1,\quad\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha

We reason with:

𝐱=α​𝐝+r​𝐮,r=1−α2,where ​𝐮∈𝐝⟂\mathbf{x}=\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\mathbf{u},\quad r=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}},\quad\text{where }\mathbf{u}\in\mathbf{d}^{\perp}
ϕ⁡(α​𝐝+r​𝐮)=(α​𝐝+r​𝐮−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(α​𝐝+r​𝐮−𝐡)\phi(\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\mathbf{u})=(\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{h})
=r2​𝐮⊤​𝚺​𝐮+2​(α​𝐝−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​r​𝐮+(α​𝐝−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(α​𝐝−𝐡)=r^{2}\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{u}+2(\alpha\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}r\mathbf{u}+(\alpha\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\alpha\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{h})

Notice that since 𝐮∈𝐝⟂\mathbf{u}\in\mathbf{d}^{\perp}, 𝐮=Π𝐝⟂​𝐮\mathbf{u}=\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{u} where Π𝐝⟂=𝐈−𝐝𝐝⊤\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^{\top} (the orthogonal projection matrix on the ortho complement of 𝐝\mathbf{d}). We can rewrite the problem as:

minϕ⁡(𝐮)s.t.‖𝐮‖=1,𝐮⊤​𝐝=0\min\quad\phi(\mathbf{u})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|\mathbf{u}\|=1,\quad\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0
ϕ⁡(𝐮)=r2​𝐮⊤​Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂​𝐮+2​r​(α​𝐝−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂​𝐮\phi(\mathbf{u})=r^{2}\mathbf{u}^{\top}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{u}+2r(\alpha\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{u}
=r2​𝐮⊤​𝐀𝐮+2​r​𝐛⊤​𝐮=r^{2}\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}+2r\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{u}

(Note: We bake the constraint 𝐮⊤​𝐝=0\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0 into 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐛\mathbf{b}).

Use Lagrange multiplier to solve optimality for ϕ⁡(𝐮)\phi(\mathbf{u}): The first order condition:

ℒ⁡(𝐮,λ,μ)=ϕ⁡(𝐮)+12​λ​(‖𝐮‖2−1)+μ⁡(𝐮⊤​𝐝)\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u},\lambda,\mu)=\phi(\mathbf{u})+\frac{1}{2}\lambda(\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}-1)+\mu(\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{d})
∇𝐮ℒ=∇𝐮ϕ​(𝐮)+λ​𝐮+μ​𝐝=0\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\mathcal{L}=\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\phi(\mathbf{u})+\lambda\mathbf{u}+\mu\mathbf{d}=0

Consider ∇𝐮ϕ​(𝐮)=2​r2​Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂​𝐮+2​r​Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​(α​𝐝−𝐡)\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\phi(\mathbf{u})=2r^{2}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{u}+2r\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\alpha\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{h}). Since Π𝐝⟂⊤​𝐝=Π𝐝⟂​𝐝=0\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{d}=0, multiplying by 𝐝⊤\mathbf{d}^{\top} implies μ=0\mu=0. Hence the Lagrangian is simplified to:

ℒ⁡(𝐮,λ)=ϕ⁡(𝐮)+λ⁡(1−‖𝐮‖)(simplified form)\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u},\lambda)=\phi(\mathbf{u})+\lambda(1-\|\mathbf{u}\|)\quad\text{(simplified form)}

The first order condition becomes:

2​r2​𝐀𝐮+2​r​𝐛=2​λ​𝐮2r^{2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}+2r\mathbf{b}=2\lambda\mathbf{u}
⇔(r2​𝐀−λ​𝐈)​𝐮=−r​𝐛\Leftrightarrow(r^{2}\mathbf{A}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{u}=-r\mathbf{b} (10)

We analyze the solution of (10) via λ\lambda. First, let’s diagonalize 𝐀=𝐐𝐃𝐐⊤\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{Q}^{\top} so that we can solve orthogonal component-wise. Notice that 𝐀\mathbf{A} is diagonalizable because it is a symmetric matrix. Let 𝐲=𝐐⊤​𝐮\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{u} and 𝐜=𝐐⊤​𝐛\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{b}. Equation (10) becomes:

r2​𝐃𝐲−λ​𝐲=−r​𝐜r^{2}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{y}-\lambda\mathbf{y}=-r\mathbf{c}
r2βiyi−λyi=−rci,i=1,…,p−2r^{2}\beta_{i}y_{i}-\lambda y_{i}=-rc_{i},\quad i=1,\dots,p-2
yi=−r​cir2​βi−λy_{i}=\frac{-rc_{i}}{r^{2}\beta_{i}-\lambda}

We enforce the constraint:

‖𝐲‖2=𝐲⊤​𝐲=𝐮⊤​𝐐𝐐⊤​𝐮=𝐮⊤​𝐮=1\|\mathbf{y}\|^{2}=\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}=1
∑i=1p−2yi2=∑i=1p−2r2​ci2(r2​βi−λ)2=1\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}y_{i}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\frac{r^{2}c_{i}^{2}}{(r^{2}\beta_{i}-\lambda)^{2}}=1
⇒(∑ir2​ci2​∏j≠i(r2​βj−λ)2)−∏kp−2(r2​βk−λ)2=0\Rightarrow\left(\sum_{i}r^{2}c_{i}^{2}\prod_{j\neq i}(r^{2}\beta_{j}-\lambda)^{2}\right)-\prod_{k}^{p-2}(r^{2}\beta_{k}-\lambda)^{2}=0 (11)

Equation (11) is a polynomial of λ\lambda with degree 2​(p−2)2(p-2). It has finite number of roots (at most 2​(p−2)2(p-2)).
