Since Ω\Omega is also connected, it must have only 1 element. Hence, 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) converges to a critical point.

A.2 Proof of Lem. 1 (Exponential Map on ℳ\mathcal{M})

Proof.

Define the center and radius

𝐜:=α​𝐝,r:=1−α2.\mathbf{c}:=\alpha\mathbf{d},\qquad r:=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}}.

For any 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} we have 𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha and ‖𝐱‖=1\|\mathbf{x}\|=1, hence

𝐱=α​𝐝+(𝐱−α​𝐝),𝐝⊤​(𝐱−α​𝐝)=0,\mathbf{x}=\alpha\mathbf{d}+(\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf{d}),\qquad\mathbf{d}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf{d})=0,

and

‖𝐱−α​𝐝‖2=‖𝐱‖2−α2=1−α2=r2.\|\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf{d}\|^{2}=\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}-\alpha^{2}=1-\alpha^{2}=r^{2}.

Thus every 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} can be written as

𝐱=𝐜+r​𝐮,with ​‖𝐮‖=1,𝐮⟂𝐝.\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{c}+r\mathbf{u},\qquad\text{with }\|\mathbf{u}\|=1,\ \mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{d}.

Therefore ℳ\mathcal{M} is a (p−2)(p-2)-dimensional sphere of radius rr centered at 𝐜\mathbf{c} in the hyperplane 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}.

Consider the map

Φ:ℳ→ℝp,Φ⁡(𝐱):=𝐮:=𝐱−𝐜r.\Phi:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{p},\qquad\Phi(\mathbf{x}):=\mathbf{u}:=\frac{\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}}{r}.

For 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}, we have ‖𝐮‖=1\|\mathbf{u}\|=1 and 𝐮⟂𝐝\mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{d}, so Φ\Phi maps ℳ\mathcal{M} diffeomorphically onto

ℳ~:={𝐮∈ℝp:∥𝐮∥=1,𝐮⟂𝐝},\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}:=\{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\|\mathbf{u}\|=1,\ \mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{d}\},

which is a standard unit sphere Sp−2S^{p-2} in 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}.

Let 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} and 𝐯∈T𝐱​ℳ\mathbf{v}\in T_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}. The differential of Φ\Phi at 𝐱\mathbf{x} is

d​Φ𝐱​(𝝃)=1r​𝝃,∀𝝃∈T𝐱​ℳ.d\Phi_{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\frac{1}{r}\,\boldsymbol{\xi},\qquad\forall\,\boldsymbol{\xi}\in T_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{M}.

Thus the corresponding tangent vector at 𝐮=Φ⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{u}=\Phi(\mathbf{x}) is

𝐰:=d​Φ𝐱​(𝐯)=1r​𝐯∈T𝐮​ℳ~.\mathbf{w}:=d\Phi_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v})=\frac{1}{r}\mathbf{v}\in T_{\mathbf{u}}\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}.

On the unit sphere ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}, geodesics are great circles. The unique geodesic 𝜸:ℝ→ℳ~\boldsymbol{\gamma}:\mathbb{R}\to\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} with initial data

𝜸⁡(0)=𝐮,𝜸′​(0)=𝐰\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0)=\mathbf{u},\qquad\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\prime}(0)=\mathbf{w}

is given by

𝜸⁡(t)=𝐮​cos⁡(‖𝐰‖​t)+𝐰‖𝐰‖​sin⁡(‖𝐰‖​t).\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)=\mathbf{u}\cos(\|\mathbf{w}\|t)+\frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\sin(\|\mathbf{w}\|t).

By definition of the exponential map on ℳ~\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},

exp𝐮ℳ~⁡(𝐰)=𝜸⁡(1)=𝐮​cos⁡(‖𝐰‖)+𝐰‖𝐰‖​sin⁡(‖𝐰‖).\exp^{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\mathbf{u}}(\mathbf{w})=\boldsymbol{\gamma}(1)=\mathbf{u}\cos(\|\mathbf{w}\|)+\frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\sin(\|\mathbf{w}\|).

To obtain the exponential map on ℳ\mathcal{M}, we pull this geodesic back via Φ−1\Phi^{-1}. Define

𝐱⁡(t):=Φ−1​(𝜸⁡(t))=𝐜+r​𝜸​(t).\mathbf{x}(t):=\Phi^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))=\mathbf{c}+r\,\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t).

Then

𝐱⁡(t)\displaystyle\mathbf{x}(t) =𝐜+r⁡[𝐮​cos⁡(‖𝐰‖​t)+𝐰‖𝐰‖​sin⁡(‖𝐰‖​t)]\displaystyle=\mathbf{c}+r\left[\mathbf{u}\cos(\|\mathbf{w}\|t)+\frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\sin(\|\mathbf{w}\|t)\right]
=𝐜+(𝐱−𝐜)​cos⁡(‖𝐰‖​t)+r​𝐰‖𝐰‖​sin⁡(‖𝐰‖​t).\displaystyle=\mathbf{c}+(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c})\cos(\|\mathbf{w}\|t)+r\,\frac{\mathbf{w}}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\sin(\|\mathbf{w}\|t).

Using 𝐰=𝐯/r\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{v}/r, we have ‖𝐰‖=‖𝐯‖/r\|\mathbf{w}\|=\|\mathbf{v}\|/r and 𝐰/‖𝐰‖=𝐯/‖𝐯‖\mathbf{w}/\|\mathbf{w}\|=\mathbf{v}/\|\mathbf{v}\|, so

𝐱⁡(t)=𝐜+(𝐱−𝐜)​cos⁡(‖𝐯‖r​t)+r​𝐯‖𝐯‖​sin⁡(‖𝐯‖r​t).\mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{c}+(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c})\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|}{r}t\Bigr)+r\,\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|}{r}t\Bigr).

By construction 𝐱⁡(0)=𝐱\mathbf{x}(0)=\mathbf{x} and 𝐱′​(0)=𝐯\mathbf{x}^{\prime}(0)=\mathbf{v}, so 𝐱⁡(t)\mathbf{x}(t) is the geodesic on ℳ\mathcal{M} starting at 𝐱\mathbf{x} with initial velocity 𝐯\mathbf{v}. Therefore

exp𝐱⁡(𝐯)=𝐱⁡(1)=𝐜+(𝐱−𝐜)​cos⁡(‖𝐯‖r)+r​𝐯‖𝐯‖​sin⁡(‖𝐯‖r).\exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{x}(1)=\mathbf{c}+(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c})\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|}{r}\Bigr)+r\,\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|}{r}\Bigr).

Substituting 𝐜=α​𝐝\mathbf{c}=\alpha\mathbf{d} and τ=‖𝐯‖/r\tau=\|\mathbf{v}\|/r gives

exp𝐱⁡(𝐯)=α​𝐝+(𝐱−α​𝐝)​cos⁡(τ)+𝐯‖𝐯‖​r​sin⁡(τ),\exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v})=\alpha\mathbf{d}+(\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf{d})\cos(\tau)+\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}\,r\sin(\tau),

which is the desired formula. ∎

A.3 Proof of Thm. 1 (Global Convergence to Optimal Steering)

A.3.1 Problem Transformation

We define the transformed variables to center the problem:

𝐮=𝐱−α​𝐝,r=1−α2\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf{d},\quad r=\sqrt{1-\alpha^{2}} (12)

The objective function on the manifold is defined as:

J⁡(𝐮)=(𝐮−𝐡~)⊤​𝚺​(𝐮−𝐡~)J(\mathbf{u})=(\mathbf{u}-\tilde{\mathbf{h}})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{u}-\tilde{\mathbf{h}}) (13)

where 𝐡~=𝐡−α​𝐝\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\mathbf{h}-\alpha\mathbf{d}.

A.3.2 Spectral Decomposition

Let (λ1,𝐯1)(\lambda_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1}) denote the smallest eigenvalue and corresponding eigenvector of the Hessian 2​𝚺2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}, representing the “flattest direction” of the quadratic valley. We decompose the shifted activation vector 𝐡~\tilde{\mathbf{h}} in the eigenbasis {𝐯i}\{\mathbf{v}_{i}\} of 2​𝚺2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}:

𝐡~=∑i=1pβi​𝐯i\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i} (14)
Case 1: β1=0\beta_{1}=0 (Orthogonal Data)

If the data vector has no component along the principal eigenvector, Lemma 3.2 of Martínez (1994) applies. 𝐡~\tilde{\mathbf{h}} is orthogonal to the eigenvector 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}, implying that a local-nonglobal minimizer does not exist. This is the trivial case where global convergence is unconditional.

Case 2: β1≠0\beta_{1}\neq 0 (General Case)

This is the nontrivial scenario. We analyze the alignment of critical points.

  1. 1.

    Initialization Alignment: The algorithm initializes at the Euclidean projection:

    𝐮0=r​𝐡~‖𝐡~‖⟹𝐯1⊤​𝐮0=r‖𝐡~‖​β1\mathbf{u}_{0}=r\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{h}}}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}\|}\implies\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{0}=\frac{r}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}\|}\beta_{1} (15)

    Consequently, the initialization preserves the sign of the data vector along the 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}:

    sgn​(𝐯1⊤​𝐮0)=sgn​(β1)\text{sgn}(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{0})=\text{sgn}(\beta_{1}) (16)
  2. 2.

    Critical Point Characterization: According to Martínez (1994), any critical point 𝐬\mathbf{s} must satisfy the secular equation:

    (2​𝚺+μ​𝐈)​𝐬=−ℓ=2​𝚺​𝐡~,(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}+\mu\mathbf{I})\mathbf{s}=-\boldsymbol{\ell}=2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}, (17)

    where ℓ:=−2​𝚺​𝐡~\boldsymbol{\ell}:=-2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\tilde{\mathbf{h}}. Since 2​𝚺=∑λi​𝐯i​𝐯i⊤2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\sum\lambda_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{\top}, where λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0 since 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} is PSD, assuming a solution of (17) has the form 𝐬=∑γi​𝐯i\mathbf{s}=\sum\gamma_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}, we match coefficients:

    (2​𝚺+μ​𝐈)​∑γi​𝐯i\displaystyle(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}+\mu\mathbf{I})\sum\gamma_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i} =∑γi​(λi+μ)​𝐯i\displaystyle=\sum\gamma_{i}(\lambda_{i}+\mu)\mathbf{v}_{i} (18)
    RHS=2​𝚺​∑βi​𝐯i\displaystyle\text{RHS}=2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\sum\beta_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i} =∑λi​βi​𝐯i\displaystyle=\sum\lambda_{i}\beta_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i} (19)

    Solving for γi\gamma_{i}:

    γi​(λi+μ)=λi​βi⟹𝐬=∑i=1pλi​βiλi+μ​𝐯i\gamma_{i}(\lambda_{i}+\mu)=\lambda_{i}\beta_{i}\implies\mathbf{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\lambda_{i}\beta_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu}\mathbf{v}_{i} (20)
  3. 3.

    Global Minimizer (𝐬G\mathbf{s}_{G}): By Martínez Theorem 3.1, the global multiplier satisfies μG≥−λ1\mu_{G}\geq-\lambda_{1}. Assuming the generic case λi+μG>0\lambda_{i}+\mu_{G}>0:

    sgn​(𝐯1⊤​𝐬G)=sgn​(β1)\text{sgn}(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{s}_{G})=\text{sgn}(\beta_{1}) (21)

    Thus, 𝐬G\mathbf{s}_{G} lies in the same spectral hemisphere as 𝐡~\tilde{\mathbf{h}}.

    Note that if λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, then following Martínez Lemma 3.2, there would be no local-nonglobal minimizer. Hence, we consider λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0.

  4. 4.

    Local-nonglobal Minimizer (𝐬L\mathbf{s}_{L}): By Martínez Lemma 3.3, a local nonglobal minimizer corresponds to μL∈(−λ2,−λ1)\mu_{L}\in(-\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{1}). This implies (λ1+μL)<0(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{L})<0, resulting in:

    sgn​(𝐯1⊤​𝐬L)=−sgn​(β1)\text{sgn}(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{s}_{L})=-\text{sgn}(\beta_{1}) (22)

A.3.3 Topological Separation Analysis

We define the the trap (So​p​pS_{opp}), the safe basin (Ss​a​m​eS_{same}), and the separating hyperplane (HH) between them:

So​p​p\displaystyle S_{opp} ={𝐮∈ℳ∣sgn​(𝐯1⊤​𝐮)=−sgn​(β1)}\displaystyle=\{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{M}\mid\text{sgn}(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u})=-\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\} (23)
Ss​a​m​e\displaystyle S_{same} ={𝐮∈ℳ∣sgn​(𝐯1⊤​𝐮)=sgn​(β1)}\displaystyle=\{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{M}\mid\text{sgn}(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u})=\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\} (24)
H\displaystyle H ={𝐮∈ℳ∣𝐯1⊤​𝐮=0}\displaystyle=\{\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{M}\mid\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u}=0\} (25)

Note that any continuous path from the initialization 𝐮0∈Ss​a​m​e\mathbf{u}_{0}\in S_{same} to the trap 𝐬L∈So​p​p\mathbf{s}_{L}\in S_{opp} must intersect HH.

Boundary Flow Analysis:

We examine the gradient flow 𝐮˙\dot{\mathbf{u}} on the boundary HH. Let 𝐰=−sgn​(β1)​𝐯1\mathbf{w}=-\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\mathbf{v}_{1} be the normal vector pointing into So​p​pS_{opp}. The projected gradient dynamics are:

𝐮˙=−Π𝐮∇J(𝐮)=−(𝐈−𝐮𝐮⊤r2)∇J(𝐮)\dot{\mathbf{u}}=-\Pi_{\mathbf{u}}\nabla J(\mathbf{u})=-\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{r^{2}}\right)\nabla J(\mathbf{u}) (26)

We project the flow onto the principal direction 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}:

𝐯1⊤​𝐮˙\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\dot{\mathbf{u}} =−𝐯1⊤(𝐈−𝐮𝐮⊤r2)∇J(𝐮)=−(𝐯1⊤−(𝐯1⊤​𝐮)​𝐮⊤r2)∇J(𝐮)\displaystyle=-\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{I}-\frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{r^{2}}\right)\nabla J(\mathbf{u})=-\left(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}-\frac{(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{r^{2}}\right)\nabla J(\mathbf{u}) (27)

For any 𝐮∈H\mathbf{u}\in H, we have 𝐯1⊤​𝐮=0\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u}=0. The expression simplifies to:

𝐯1⊤𝐮˙=−𝐯1⊤∇J(𝐮)\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\dot{\mathbf{u}}=-\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\nabla J(\mathbf{u}) (28)

By checking the flow relative to the “bad” direction 𝐰\mathbf{w}, we have:

𝐰⊤​𝐮˙\displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{\top}\dot{\mathbf{u}} =−sgn(β1)(𝐯1⊤𝐮˙)=sgn(β1)𝐯1⊤∇J(𝐮)=sgn(β1)𝐯1⊤(2𝚺𝐮−ℓ)\displaystyle=-\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\dot{\mathbf{u}})=\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\nabla J(\mathbf{u})=\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol{\ell}) (29)
=sgn​(β1)​𝐯1⊤​(2​𝚺)​𝐮−sgn​(β1)​𝐯1⊤​ℓ\displaystyle=\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\mathbf{u}-\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\ell} (30)

Analyzing the two terms:

  1. 1.

    𝐯1⊤​(2​𝚺)=λ1​𝐯1⊤⟹𝐯1⊤​(2​𝚺)​𝐮=λ1​(𝐯1⊤​𝐮)=0\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\lambda_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\implies\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\mathbf{u}=\lambda_{1}(\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{u})=0 (since 𝐮∈H\mathbf{u}\in H).

  2. 2.

    𝐯1⊤​ℓ=−𝐯1⊤​(2​𝚺)​𝐡~=−λ1​β1\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\ell}=-\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top}(2\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=-\lambda_{1}\beta_{1}.

Substituting back:

𝐰⊤​𝐮˙=0−sgn​(β1)​(−λ1​β1)=−λ1​|β1|\mathbf{w}^{\top}\dot{\mathbf{u}}=0-\text{sgn}(\beta_{1})(-\lambda_{1}\beta_{1})=-\lambda_{1}|\beta_{1}| (31)

Since λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 and |β1|>0|\beta_{1}|>0, we have:

𝐰⊤​𝐮˙<0∀𝐮∈H\mathbf{w}^{\top}\dot{\mathbf{u}}<0\quad\forall\mathbf{u}\in H (32)

Conclusion: To get to the trap So​p​pS_{opp}, any gradient flow must intersect HH, but the gradient at the intersection point strictly points away from So​p​pS_{opp} (the basin of the local minimizer) and towards Ss​a​m​eS_{same}. Therefore, the trajectory starting at 𝐮0\mathbf{u}_{0} can not reach So​p​pS_{opp} and will be attract to Ss​a​m​eS_{same}. Hence it must converge to the global minimizer 𝐬G\mathbf{s}_{G}.

A.4 Proof of Proposition 1 (Choice of Step-size)

JJ is a LL-smooth with L:=2​‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂‖2L:=2\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\|_{2}.

Since T𝐱M={𝝃∈ℝp:𝐱⊤𝝃=0,𝐝⊤𝝃=0}T_{\mathbf{x}}M=\{\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0,\ \mathbf{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0\}, hence 𝐝⊤​𝝃=0\mathbf{d}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}=0, so 𝝃∈𝐝⟂⟹Π𝐝⟂​𝝃=𝝃.\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbf{d}^{\perp}\implies\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\xi}. Therefore,

𝝃⊤​𝚺​𝝃=(Π𝐝⟂​𝝃)⊤​𝚺​(Π𝐝⟂​𝝃)=𝝃⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂)​𝝃.\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\boldsymbol{\xi})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\boldsymbol{\xi})=\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}})\boldsymbol{\xi}. (33)

Since Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}} is symmetric PSD on 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}, its Rayleigh quotient is bounded by its spectral norm:

𝝃⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂)​𝝃≤‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂‖2​‖𝝃‖2.\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}})\boldsymbol{\xi}\leq\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\|_{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|^{2}. (34)

Because JJ is quadratic, ∇2J​(𝐱)=2​𝚺\nabla^{2}J(\mathbf{x})=2\mathbf{\Sigma}, for all 𝐱.\mathbf{x}. Therefore,

𝝃⊤​∇2J​(𝐱)​𝝃=2​𝝃⊤​𝚺​𝝃≤2​‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂‖2​‖𝝃‖2.\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\top}\nabla^{2}J(\mathbf{x})\boldsymbol{\xi}=2\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\xi}\leq 2\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\|_{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|^{2}. (35)

This proves the claim with L:=2​‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚺​Π𝐝⟂‖2L:=2\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Sigma}\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\|_{2}.

Derive the bound for step-size η\eta.

Consider the geodesic γ⁡(τ):=exp𝐱t​(τ​𝝃t)\gamma(\tau):=\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}(\tau\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}). Since the velocity γ˙\dot{\gamma} is tangent to MM, Eqn. 35 applies, bounding the second derivative of the objective JJ along the path by d2d​τ2​J​(γ⁡(τ))≤L​‖γ˙​(τ)‖2\frac{d^{2}}{d\tau^{2}}J(\gamma(\tau))\leq L\|\dot{\gamma}(\tau)\|^{2}. This implies the quadratic upper bound:

J⁡(γ⁡(η))≤J⁡(𝐱t)+η⁡⟨grad​J​(𝐱t),𝝃t⟩+L​η22​‖𝝃t‖2.J(\gamma(\eta))\leq J(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\eta\langle\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t}),\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}\|^{2}.

Substituting 𝝃t=−grad​J​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}=-\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t}) and noting ‖𝝃t‖=‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖\|\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}\|=\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|, we obtain J⁡(𝐱t+1)≤J⁡(𝐱t)−η⁡(1−L​η2)​‖grad ​J​(𝐱t)‖2J(\mathbf{x}_{t+1})\leq J(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\eta(1-\frac{L\eta}{2})\|\text{grad }J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}. Since η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L implies 1−L​η2≥121-\frac{L\eta}{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}, the descent condition holds.

This proves the Prop. 1

A.5 Proof of Sublinear Stationarity Rate

Corollary 1 (Sublinear stationarity rate).

Under the assumptions of Prop. 1, for any horizon T≥1T\geq 1,

min0≤t<T⁡‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖≤2​(J⁡(𝐱0)−J∗)η​T=O⁡(1T),\min_{0\leq t<T}\|\mathrm{grad}\,J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2(J(\mathbf{x}_{0})-J^{*})}{\eta T}}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right),

where J∗:=min𝐱∈ℳ⁡J⁡(𝐱)J^{*}:=\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}J(\mathbf{x}).

The proof of Cor. 1 is provided in App. A.5.

Although the O⁡(1/T)O(1/\sqrt{T}) rate is the best guarantee for potentially degenerate landscapes, we can achieve significantly faster local convergence by regularizing the collateral metric. The proof for Rem. 3 is provided in App. 3. From Proposition 1, the iterates satisfy the descent inequality J⁡(𝐱t+1)≤J⁡(𝐱t)−η2​‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖2J(\mathbf{x}_{t+1})\leq J(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\frac{\eta}{2}\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}. Summing this over t=0,…,T−1t=0,\dots,T-1 yields:

J⁡(𝐱T)≤J⁡(𝐱0)−η2​∑t=0T−1‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖2.J(\mathbf{x}_{T})\leq J(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}.

Noting that J⁡(𝐱T)≥J∗J(\mathbf{x}_{T})\geq J^{*}, we have ∑t=0T−1‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖2≤2η​(J⁡(𝐱0)−J∗)\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2}{\eta}(J(\mathbf{x}_{0})-J^{*}). Since minimum of a set is bounded by its average (mint⁡at≤1T​∑at\min_{t}a_{t}\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum a_{t}), we obtain:

min0≤t<T⁡‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖2≤1T​∑t=0T−1‖grad​J​(𝐱t)‖2≤2​(J⁡(𝐱0)−J∗)η​T.\min_{0\leq t<T}\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\|\mathrm{grad}J(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2(J(\mathbf{x}_{0})-J^{*})}{\eta T}.

Taking the square root completes the proof.

A.6 Proof of Linear Convergence via Regularization

Remark 3 (Linear convergence via regularization).

The O⁡(1/T)O(1/\sqrt{T}) rate is standard when the objective curvature may be flat along some feasible directions, which can occur when 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} is low-rank. To obtain a local linear convergence rate, one can regularize the objective by adding a small isotropic penalty on 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}:

𝚺ε:=𝚺+ε​Π𝐝⟂,ε>0,Π𝐝⟂=𝐈−𝐝𝐝⊤.\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}:=\mathbf{\Sigma}+\varepsilon\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}},\qquad\varepsilon>0,\qquad\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^{\top}.

Detailed Statemment

Define the regularized objective

Jε​(𝐱):=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺ε​(𝐱−𝐡),𝚺ε:=𝚺+ε​Π𝐝⟂,ε>0,J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}):=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}),\quad\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}:=\mathbf{\Sigma}+\varepsilon\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}},\quad\varepsilon>0,

on the same manifold MM. Let 𝐱ε∗\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*} be a (global) minimizer of JεJ_{\varepsilon} on MM. Assume the Riemannian Hessian of JεJ_{\varepsilon} at 𝐱ε∗\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*} is positive definite on the tangent space, i.e., there exists με>0\mu_{\varepsilon}>0 such that

⟨𝝃,Hess​Jε​(𝐱ε∗)​[𝝃]⟩≥με​‖𝝃‖2∀𝝃∈T𝐱ε∗​M.\langle\boldsymbol{\xi},\text{Hess}\,J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})[\boldsymbol{\xi}]\rangle\geq\mu_{\varepsilon}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|^{2}\quad\forall\boldsymbol{\xi}\in T_{\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*}}M. (36)

Then there exists a neighborhood 𝒩\mathcal{N} of 𝐱ε∗\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*} such that if Algorithm 1 is run on JεJ_{\varepsilon} with a sufficiently small step size η∈(0,η¯]\eta\in(0,\bar{\eta}] and initialization 𝐱0∈𝒩\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathcal{N}, the iterates satisfy linear convergence:

Jε​(𝐱t)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗)≤(1−η​με)t​(Jε​(𝐱0)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗)).J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\leq(1-\eta\mu_{\varepsilon})^{t}\left(J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{0})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\right). (37)

Proof

Condition (36) is the Riemannian analogue of strong convexity (restricted to the tangent space). It implies a local Polyak–Łojasiewicz-type inequality in a neighborhood of 𝐱ε∗\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*}:

‖grad​Jε​(𝐱)‖2≥2​με​(Jε​(𝐱)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗)),∀𝐱∈𝒩.\|\text{grad}\,J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}\geq 2\mu_{\varepsilon}\left(J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\right),\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{N}. (38)

On the other hand, JεJ_{\varepsilon} is smooth on MM, so the same one-step descent bound as before holds locally:

Jε​(𝐱t+1)≤Jε​(𝐱t)−η⁡(1−Lε​η2)​‖grad​Jε​(𝐱t)‖2∀𝐱t∈𝒩,J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t+1})\leq J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\eta\left(1-\frac{L_{\varepsilon}\eta}{2}\right)\|\text{grad}\,J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}\quad\forall\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathcal{N}, (39)

for some local smoothness constant LεL_{\varepsilon}. Choose η≤1/Lε\eta\leq 1/L_{\varepsilon}, so the bracket is at least 1/21/2, giving

Jε​(𝐱t+1)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗)≤(Jε​(𝐱t)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗))−η2​‖grad​Jε​(𝐱t)‖2.J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t+1})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\leq\left(J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\right)-\frac{\eta}{2}\|\text{grad}\,J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\|^{2}. (40)

Finally apply (38) to (40):

Jε​(𝐱t+1)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗)≤(1−η​με)​(Jε​(𝐱t)−Jε​(𝐱ε∗)),J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t+1})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\leq(1-\eta\mu_{\varepsilon})\left(J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-J_{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\varepsilon}^{*})\right),

and iterate the inequality to obtain (37).

Appendix B Derivation of special cases.

B.1 Derive Worst-Colateral Damage with 𝐝\mathbf{d}-Orthogonal Features

Orthogonal-features assumption. Other features 𝐟\mathbf{f} live in the subspace 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}. Since we do not know the true feature set, we take a conservative worst-case bound over all unit directions in 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}:

(collateral bound)sup‖𝐟‖=1,𝐟⊤​𝐝=0(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2.(\text{collateral bound})\quad\sup_{\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}. (41)

Note that the maximizer 𝐟\mathbf{f} is a real feature—but serves as a upper bound over other features directions. In this case, since we assume that we might not know exactly where the other features live. To be safe, we will minimize the magnitude of our shift in all directions where a feature could potentially be.

Equivalance in objective Let 𝚫:=𝐱−𝐡\mathbf{\Delta}:=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}. Split 𝚫\mathbf{\Delta} into components parallel and orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}: 𝚫=(𝐝⊤​𝚫)​𝐝+Π𝐝⟂​𝚫,Π𝐝⟂:=𝐈−𝐝𝐝⊤.\mathbf{\Delta}=(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})\mathbf{d}+\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta},\quad\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}:=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^{\top}.

Now take any direction 𝐟\mathbf{f} with 𝐟⊤​𝐝=0\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0 (so 𝐟∈𝐝⟂\mathbf{f}\in\mathbf{d}^{\perp}). Then

𝐟⊤​𝚫=𝐟⊤​((𝐝⊤​𝚫)​𝐝)+𝐟⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚫)=(𝐝⊤​𝚫)​(𝐟⊤​𝐝)⏟0+𝐟⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚫)=𝐟⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚫).\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}=\mathbf{f}^{\top}((\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})\mathbf{d})+\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta})=\underbrace{(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})(\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d})}_{0}+\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta})=\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta}). (42)

So the worst-case bound becomes

sup‖𝐟‖=1,𝐟⊤​𝐝=0(𝐟⊤​𝚫)2=sup‖𝐟‖=1,𝐟∈𝐝⟂(𝐟⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚫))2.\sup_{\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})^{2}=\sup_{\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\mathbf{f}\in\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta}))^{2}. (43)

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz in the subspace 𝐝⟂\mathbf{d}^{\perp}:

|𝐟⊤​(Π𝐝⟂​𝚫)|≤‖𝐟‖​‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚫‖=‖Π𝐝⟂​𝚫‖.|\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta})|\leq\|\mathbf{f}\|\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta}\|=\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta}\|. (44)

Therefore,

sup‖𝐟‖=1,𝐟⊤​𝐝=0(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2=‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2.\sup_{\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}=\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}. (45)

So the simplified objective becomes

min𝐱∈ℳ,‖𝐱‖=1,𝐱⊤​𝐝=α⁡‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2.\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M},||\mathbf{x}||=1,\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=\alpha}\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}. (46)

Solution Use the parameterization 𝐱=α​𝐝+r​𝐮\mathbf{x}=\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\mathbf{u} with 𝐮⟂𝐝,‖𝐮‖=1\mathbf{u}\perp\mathbf{d},\|\mathbf{u}\|=1. Let 𝐡⟂:=Π𝐝⟂​𝐡=𝐡−(𝐝⊤​𝐡)​𝐝\mathbf{h}_{\perp}:=\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}.

The objective simplifies as follows:

‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2=‖r​𝐮−𝐡⟂‖2\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}=\|r\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{h}_{\perp}\|^{2} (47)
=r2​‖𝐮‖2+‖𝐡⟂‖2−2​r​𝐮⊤​𝐡⟂=r2+‖𝐡⟂‖2−2​r​𝐮⊤​𝐡⟂=r^{2}\|\mathbf{u}\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{h}_{\perp}\|^{2}-2r\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{\perp}=r^{2}+\|\mathbf{h}_{\perp}\|^{2}-2r\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{\perp} (48)

Minimizing this is equivalent to maximizing 𝐮⊤​𝐡⟂\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{\perp}. By Cauchy–Schwarz, the maximum is reached when 𝐮\mathbf{u} aligns with 𝐡⟂\mathbf{h}_{\perp}:

𝐮∗=𝐡⟂‖𝐡⟂‖(if ​𝐡⟂≠𝟎)\mathbf{u}^{*}=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{\perp}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{\perp}\|}\quad(\text{if }\mathbf{h}_{\perp}\neq\mathbf{0}) (49)

The optimal solution is thus:

𝐱∗=α​𝐝+r​𝐡−(𝐝⊤​𝐡)​𝐝‖𝐡−(𝐝⊤​𝐡)​𝐝‖\mathbf{x}^{*}=\alpha\mathbf{d}+r\frac{\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{h}-(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h})\mathbf{d}\|} (50)

B.2 Derive Worst-Collateral Damage with 𝐝\mathbf{d}-Near-Orthogonal Features

Near-orthogonal other features. Instead of requiring 𝐟⊤​𝐝=0\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}=0, a small overlap is allowed:

‖𝐟‖=1,|𝐟⊤​𝐝|≤ε​,\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,\quad|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}|\leq\varepsilon\text{,} (51)

where ε∈[0,1)\varepsilon\in[0,1) is small.

Worst-case collateral objective (same style as the remark):

min⁡sup‖𝐟‖=1,|𝐟⊤​𝐝|≤ε𝐱∈ℳ⁡(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2​.\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\sup_{\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}|\leq\varepsilon}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}\text{.} (52)

As before, this is a worst-case bound over directions; it is not assumed that the maximizer 𝐟\mathbf{f} is an actual feature.

Equivalence of objective function Similar to the 𝐝\mathbf{d}-orthogonal case, 𝚫:=𝐱−𝐡\mathbf{\Delta}:=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}. Decompose 𝚫\mathbf{\Delta} into parts parallel and orthogonal to 𝐝\mathbf{d}:

  • •

    parallel scalar: β:=𝐝⊤​𝚫=𝐝⊤​𝐱−𝐝⊤​𝐡=α−𝐝⊤​𝐡\beta:=\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}=\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h}=\alpha-\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h}.

  • •

    orthogonal part: 𝚫⟂:=Π𝐝⟂​𝚫=Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)\mathbf{\Delta}_{\perp}:=\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}\mathbf{\Delta}=\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}).

Important point: because 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} forces 𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha, the scalar β\beta is constant over all feasible 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Taking any feasible 𝐟\mathbf{f} with ‖𝐟‖=1\|\mathbf{f}\|=1 and |𝐟⊤​𝐝|≤ε|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}|\leq\varepsilon, we denote: a⁡(𝐟):=𝐟⊤​𝐝(|a⁡(𝐟)|≤ε)a(\mathbf{f}):=\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}\quad(|a(\mathbf{f})|\leq\varepsilon). Then 𝐟\mathbf{f} can be decomposed as:

𝐟=a⁡(𝐟)​𝐝+1−a​(𝐟)2​𝐮f,where ​𝐮f⟂𝐝,‖𝐮f‖=1​.\mathbf{f}=a(\mathbf{f})\mathbf{d}+\sqrt{1-a(\mathbf{f})^{2}}\mathbf{u}_{f},\quad\text{where }\mathbf{u}_{f}\perp\mathbf{d},\|\mathbf{u}_{f}\|=1\text{.} (53)

Therefore:

𝐟⊤​𝚫=a⁡(𝐟)​(𝐝⊤​𝚫)+1−a​(𝐟)2​𝐮f⊤​𝚫⟂=a⁡(𝐟)​β+1−a​(𝐟)2​𝐮f⊤​𝚫⟂​.\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}=a(\mathbf{f})(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})+\sqrt{1-a(\mathbf{f})^{2}}\mathbf{u}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}_{\perp}=a(\mathbf{f})\beta+\sqrt{1-a(\mathbf{f})^{2}}\mathbf{u}_{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}_{\perp}\text{.} (54)

For any fixed aa, the worst case over 𝐮f\mathbf{u}_{f} is achieved by aligning 𝐮f\mathbf{u}_{f} with 𝚫⟂\mathbf{\Delta}_{\perp}, giving:

sup𝐮f⟂𝐝,‖𝐮f‖=1|𝐟⊤​𝚫|=|a||β|+1−a2​‖𝚫⟂‖​.\sup_{\mathbf{u}_{f}\perp\mathbf{d},\|\mathbf{u}_{f}\|=1}|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}|=|a||\beta|+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\|\mathbf{\Delta}_{\perp}\|\text{.} (55)

Therefore the whole supremum becomes a maximization over aa:

sup‖𝐟‖=1,|𝐟⊤​𝐝|≤ε|𝐟⊤​𝚫|=max0≤a≤ε⁡(a​|β|+1−a2​‖𝚫⟂‖)​.\sup_{\|\mathbf{f}\|=1,|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{d}|\leq\varepsilon}|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}|=\max_{0\leq a\leq\varepsilon}\left(a|\beta|+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\|\mathbf{\Delta}_{\perp}\|\right)\text{.} (56)

Since sup(𝐟⊤​𝚫)2=(sup|𝐟⊤​𝚫|)2\sup(\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})^{2}=(\sup|\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta}|)^{2}, the 𝐝\mathbf{d}-near-orthogonal objective becomes:

min𝐱∈ℳ⁡[max0≤a≤ε⁡(a​|β|+1−a2​‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖)]2​.\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\left[\max_{0\leq a\leq\varepsilon}\left(a|\beta|+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|\right)\right]^{2}\text{.} (57)

Since |β|=|α−𝐝⊤​𝐡||\beta|=|\alpha-\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h}| is a constant, the only 𝐱\mathbf{x}-dependence component in the objective is:

A⁡(𝐱):=‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖.A(\mathbf{x}):=\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|. (58)

Solution Monotonicity fact. For any fixed a∈[0,ε]a\in[0,\varepsilon], the expression a​|β|+1−a2​A​(𝐱)a|\beta|+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}A(\mathbf{x}) is an increasing function of A⁡(𝐱)A(\mathbf{x}). A maximum of increasing functions is also increasing, and squaring preserves the argmin since everything is nonnegative. Hence, minimizing the objective over 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M} is equivalent to minimizing A⁡(𝐱)=‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖A(\mathbf{x})=\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\| over 𝐱∈ℳ\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}, for any fixed aa.

That means the near-orthogonal problem has exactly the same minimizers in Eqn. 7 as the orthogonal case min𝐱∈ℳ⁡‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}.

B.3 Uniform features on a sphere

Instead of the conservative worst-case over 𝐟\mathbf{f}, we assume the collateral direction 𝐟\mathbf{f} is random and uniform on the unit sphere in ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}. The expected collateral damage objective is:

min𝐱∈ℳ⁡𝔼𝐟​[(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2].\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{f}}\left[(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}\right].

The expectation expands as: 𝔼⁡[(𝐟⊤​𝚫)2]=𝔼⁡[𝚫⊤​(𝐟𝐟⊤)​𝚫]=𝚫⊤​𝔼​[𝐟𝐟⊤]​𝚫.\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{f}^{\top}\mathbf{\Delta})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{\Delta}^{\top}(\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^{\top})\mathbf{\Delta}]=\mathbf{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^{\top}]\mathbf{\Delta}. Since the uniform distribution on a sphere is rotationally invariant, the second moment matrix is isotropic:

𝔼⁡[𝐟𝐟⊤]=1p​𝐈.\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^{\top}]=\frac{1}{p}\mathbf{I}.

Substituting this back, the objective becomes minimizing the squared Euclidean distance:

𝔼⁡[(𝐟⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2]=1p​‖𝐱−𝐡‖2.\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{f}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2}]=\frac{1}{p}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}\|^{2}.

Again, since 𝐝⊤​(𝐱−𝐡)=α−𝐝⊤​𝐡\mathbf{d}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})=\alpha-\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h} is a constant and

‖𝐱−𝐡‖2=‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2+(𝐝⊤​(𝐱−𝐡))2,\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}\|^{2}=\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}+(\mathbf{d}^{\top}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}))^{2},

Hence, minimizing the total distance ‖𝐱−𝐡‖2\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}\|^{2} over ℳ\mathcal{M} is exactly equivalent to minimizing ‖Π𝐝⟂​(𝐱−𝐡)‖2\|\Pi_{\mathbf{d}^{\perp}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})\|^{2}, yielding the unique SLERP point in span​{𝐡,𝐝}\text{span}\{\mathbf{h},\mathbf{d}\} as the solution.

Appendix C More experiment details

C.1 Models.

We evaluate across a diverse set of instruction-tuned LLMs spanning model families and scales: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), and Gemma-2-9B-it (Gemma Team et al., 2024). All results are reported using the official tokenizers and checkpointed weights.

C.2 Intervention locations.

We perform activation steering by editing hidden states at intervention locations, positioned after the layer normalization of the attention and MLP layers, results in 2​L2L locations, where LL is the number of model’s layers. We apply this setting to all methods for a fair comparison.

C.3 Target direction construction.

We precompute the steering direction 𝐝ℓ\mathbf{d}_{\ell} for each intervention location using a calibration dataset following the Angular Steering protocol. We define 𝒟harmful\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}} using an 80% split of AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023b) with 416 harmful instructions and 𝒟harmless\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmless}} using randomly sampled 512 harmless instructions from Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023).

Let 𝐡ℓ,t​(x)∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the activation at layer ℓ\ell and token position tt, and let 𝐡^ℓ,t​(x)=𝐡ℓ,t​(x)/‖𝐡ℓ,t​(x)‖\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{\ell,t}(x)=\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}(x)/\|\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}(x)\| denote its unit-normalized version. Here, we omit sub-layer indices for simplicity. We compute the normalized mean activations for each class: μharmful=1|𝒟harmful|​∑x∈𝒟harmful𝐡^ℓ,t​(x),μharmless=1|𝒟harmless|​∑x∈𝒟harmless𝐡^ℓ,t​(x),\mu_{\mathrm{harmful}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmful}}}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{\ell,t}(x),\qquad\mu_{\mathrm{harmless}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmless}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harmless}}}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{\ell,t}(x), The feature direction is then defined by the standard difference-in-means estimator (Belrose, 2023), 𝐝ℓ∝μharmful−μharmless\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\propto\mu_{\mathrm{harmful}}-\mu_{\mathrm{harmless}}, renormalized to unit length. This yields a different steering direction for each of the 2​L2L locations. We use these intervention location-specific directions, whereas for Angular Steering, we keep their selection rule for a single direction to apply across all locations.

C.4 Collateral matrix estimation and optimization hyperparameters.

We precompute the collateral matrix using the activation second moment, denoted 𝚺𝐡ref,ℓ\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}},\ell} for layer ℓ\ell (omitting sub-layer indices). For each intervention location, we collect N=100,000N=100{,}000 token activations from the C4 corpus (Raffel et al., 2020). Applying the same unit-normalization as in the target direction construction, we compute the empirical second moment at layer ℓ\ell as 𝚺𝐡ref,ℓ=1N​∑i=1N𝐡ref^ℓ,i​𝐡ref^ℓ,i⊤.\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}},\ell}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}}_{\ell,i}\hat{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}}}_{\ell,i}^{\top}. While we use C4 here, other corpus can be chosen to reflect specific task priorities or user preferences, as it defines which feature directions are costly to perturb.

To ensure scale insensitivity across layers and models, we normalize the matrix by its top eigenvalue, 𝚺𝐡,ℓ←𝚺𝐡ref,ℓ/λmax​(𝚺𝐡ref,ℓ)\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h},\ell}\leftarrow\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}},\ell}/\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}},\ell}). Since this ensures ‖𝚺𝐡ref,ℓ‖2=1\|\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{h_{\text{ref}}},\ell}\|_{2}=1, Prop. 1 implies that any step size η∈(0,0.5]\eta\in(0,0.5] guarantees objective decrease. In all experiments, we set η=0.3\eta=0.3 and use T=1T=1 iteration for efficiency, finding that a single geodesic step is sufficient for strong performance.

C.5 Baselines.

We compare our method to the following steering operators: (i) SLERP, which interpolates on the unit sphere toward the target direction; (ii) Angular Steering, which rotates activations within a fixed 2D steering plane to a target in-plane angle; and (iii) ActAdd, with a scalar coefficient λ\lambda controlling strength, and (iv) No steering.

C.6 Steering strength.

Different baselines expose different knobs: SLERP/COAST naturally accept an alignment target expressed as a cosine similarity with 𝐝ℓ\mathbf{d}_{\ell}, ActAdd uses an additive coefficient, and Angular Steering controls a rotation angle in a chosen 2D plane. To enable comparison with angular steering by degree of steered, we match methods using a common angular strength parameter. Specifically, we sweep an angle budget θ∈[0∘,180∘]\theta\in[0^{\circ},180^{\circ}] and define the corresponding cosine target α=cos⁡(θ)\alpha=\cos(\theta). Restricting θ\theta to [0∘,180∘][0^{\circ},180^{\circ}] avoids cosine aliasing on [0∘,360∘][0^{\circ},360^{\circ}] (distinct angles can share the same cosine), while spanning the full range of cosine targets from +1+1 to −1-1. For Angular Steering, the method control steering directly by a target in-plane angle after projecting onto the steering plane. For actadd, we steer with coefficient from -10 to 10, each interval of 1.

C.7 Adaptive Alignment Budget.

A single global target α\alpha applied uniformly to all tokens and layers can be overly strict: tokens whose pre-steering activation is nearly orthogonal to 𝐝ℓ\mathbf{d}_{\ell} would be forced to undergo a large rotation, which can introduce unnecessary collateral change. To make steering more context-sensitive while keeping a single user-facing control parameter, we set the constraint for SLERP/COAST at each (ℓ,t)(\ell,t) as αℓ,t=α⋅|⟨𝐡ℓ,t,𝐝ℓ⟩|\alpha_{\ell,t}\;=\;\alpha\cdot\bigl|\langle\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t},\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\rangle\bigr| where 𝐡ℓ,t=𝐡ℓ,t/‖𝐡ℓ,t‖\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}=\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}/\|\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}\|. Intuitively, this allocates more steering budget to states that already express the target feature (large |⟨𝐡ℓ,t,𝐝ℓ⟩||\langle\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t},\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\rangle|) and imposes a tighter constraint on unrelated states, reducing unnecessary global distortion.

C.8 Norm preservation for spherical steering (SLERP/COAST).

SLERP and COAST operate on the unit sphere to preserve directionality while controlling angular displacement. To preserve the original activation scale, we implement both methods by (1) normalizing the activation, (2) performing the spherical steering update on h^ℓ,t\hat{h}_{\ell,t} to obtain x^ℓ,t\hat{x}_{\ell,t}, and then (3) rescaling back to the original norm: xℓ,t=‖hℓ,t‖⋅x^ℓ,tx_{\ell,t}\;=\;\|h_{\ell,t}\|\cdot\hat{x}_{\ell,t}.

Appendix D Computational Cost Analysis.

To validate the practical feasibility of our approach, we evaluate the inference throughput (tokens per second) across all methods using the official implementations. As reported in Table 2, the overhead introduced by steering is minimal. While COAST involves slight additional computational cost due to the per-token normalization and rescaling operations—resulting in a throughput reduction of approximately 0.9% to 4.0% compared to the unsteered baseline—this overhead is small in practice. The method maintains high-speed generation, confirming that COAST is well-suited for real-time deployment where both safety and low latency are critical.

Appendix E Solution for Collateral-damage Minimizing Activation Steering via KKT Conditions

Problem Formulation Recall. Given an activation vector 𝐡∈ℝp\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, a steering direction 𝐝∈ℝp\mathbf{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} with ‖𝐝‖=1\|\mathbf{d}\|=1, and a target alignment α∈(𝐝⊤​𝐡,1]\alpha\in(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{h},1], we seek a steered activation 𝐱\mathbf{x} that minimizes collateral damage while achieving the desired alignment:

min𝐱\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{x}} J⁡(𝐱)=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)\displaystyle J(\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h}) (59)
s.t.\displaystyle\textrm{s.t.} ‖𝐱‖2=1\displaystyle\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}=1
𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\displaystyle\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha

where 𝚺=𝔼⁡[𝐡𝐡⊤]\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h}\mathbf{h}^{\top}] is the empirical second-moment matrix of activations, computed from a reference corpus. The objective J⁡(𝐱)J(\mathbf{x}) measures the expected squared change along feature directions, weighted by the activation covariance. The constraints ensure unit norm (preserving activation magnitude) and target alignment with the steering direction.

Closed-Form Solution via KKT Conditions. In the main paper, we solve (59) using Riemannian gradient descent (Alg. 1). Here we derive an equivalent closed-form solution via the KKT conditions. The Lagrangian with multipliers λ\lambda and μ\mu for the norm and alignment constraints is:

ℒ⁡(𝐱,λ,μ)=(𝐱−𝐡)⊤​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)+λ⁡(‖𝐱‖2−1)+μ⁡(𝐝⊤​𝐱−α)\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x},\lambda,\mu)=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})+\lambda(\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}-1)+\mu(\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}-\alpha) (60)

Setting ∇𝐱ℒ=2​𝚺​(𝐱−𝐡)+2​λ​𝐱+μ​𝐝=0\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\mathcal{L}=2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{h})+2\lambda\mathbf{x}+\mu\mathbf{d}=0 and rearranging:

𝐱⁡(λ,μ)=(𝚺+λ​𝐈)−1​(𝚺​𝐡−μ2​𝐝)\mathbf{x}(\lambda,\mu)=(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{h}-\frac{\mu}{2}\mathbf{d}\right) (61)

To find 𝐱\mathbf{x}, it remains to determine the Lagrange multipliers λ\lambda and μ\mu. We can eliminate μ\mu by using the alignment constraint. Let 𝚺=𝐐​𝚲​𝐐⊤\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^{\top} be the eigendecomposition with 𝚲=diag​(σ1,…,σp)\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\text{diag}(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{p}), and define 𝐡~=𝐐⊤​𝐡\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{h} and 𝐝~=𝐐⊤​𝐝\tilde{\mathbf{d}}=\mathbf{Q}^{\top}\mathbf{d} as the representations in the eigenbasis. Substituting (61) into 𝐝⊤​𝐱=α\mathbf{d}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\alpha and solving for μ\mu results in

μ⁡(λ)=2​(A​(λ)−α)B⁡(λ),\mu(\lambda)=\frac{2(A(\lambda)-\alpha)}{B(\lambda)}, (62)

where

A⁡(λ)=∑i=1pσi​d~i​h~iσi+λ,B⁡(λ)=∑i=1pd~i2σi+λ.A(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\sigma_{i}\tilde{d}_{i}\tilde{h}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}+\lambda},\quad B(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\tilde{d}_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}+\lambda}. (63)

Substituting μ⁡(λ)\mu(\lambda) back into (61) and applying the norm constraint ‖𝐱‖2=1\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}=1, we obtain a scalar equation in λ\lambda:

G⁡(λ)=∑i=1p(σi​h~i−μ⁡(λ)2​d~iσi+λ)2−1=0G(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}\tilde{h}_{i}-\frac{\mu(\lambda)}{2}\tilde{d}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}+\lambda}\right)^{2}-1=0 (64)

Solving G⁡(λ)=0G(\lambda)=0 for λ∗\lambda^{*} then gives μ∗\mu^{*} via (62) and 𝐱\mathbf{x} via (61). Standard root-finding methods such as Brent’s or Newton’s method can be used. The eigendecomposition of 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} can be precomputed once per layer, and for each 𝐡\mathbf{h}, the cost reduces to two matrix-vector products with 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and a one-dimensional search.
